title: Body fat optimizes rodent survival in a stochastic dryland ecosystem
content:
Using 10 years of field data, we identify the mechanistic pathway linking climate-driven resource landscapes to survival through diet and body fat, revealing how environmental conditions, individual dietary choice and body fat shape survival of rodents in a stochastic desert ecosystem.


Abstract

Climate change is rapidly altering the timing, quantity and variability of precipitation in dryland ecosystems with direct effects on the composition and abundance of primary producer and consumer communities. However, the causal mechanisms linking primary productivity to animal survival are rarely studied. Dryland ecosystems are highly sensitive to climate change, with pronounced declines in primary production and increasing variability in plant community composition. Specifically, variation in rainfall creates resource landscapes that differ in primary producer abundance, composition and nutritional quality, and consumers respond to these altered resource landscapes with changes in diet, body condition and ultimately survival. Dryland ecosystems therefore provide a natural context for testing the causal pathways linking climate-driven variation in primary productivity to changes in consumer diets, body condition and survival. We combined 10 years of longitudinal data on precipitation and plant biomass with paired measurements of individual diet and percent body fat from a community of granivorous desert rodents (Heteromyidae) using structural equation modelling to untangle the pathway(s) linking seasonal climate variation to consumer body fat. We then used Cormack–Jolly–Seber models to quantify the effects of percent body fat on apparent survival as a measure of individual fitness. We observed contrasting resource pathways between C3 and C4 primary producers: C3 plant growth was influenced by season and precipitation, while C4 plant growth was mediated primarily by precipitation. Consistent with predictions, rodents that consumed higher quality C3 plants stored more body fat, but the link between body fat and survival varied among taxa as kangaroo rat survival decreased beyond a threshold of ~6%–7% body fat, while pocket mice exhibited no relationship. These findings illustrate that climate-mediated resource composition and abundance modulate diet by consumers, and our models reveal a direct pathway linking body condition to diet and the consumption of high-quality C3 resources. Further, we show that body condition does not linearly increase survival, likely due to differences in life-history traits such as caching behaviour and mode of locomotion. Collectively, these results emphasize that individual survival likely emerges from interactions between resource landscapes, diet and consumer physiology.
